connection: ClockEntryRepository stores entries in a private List and returns employee entries, while callers need only enumerate them. Narrow repository query results to IEnumerable<ClockEntry> so consumers depend on enumeration rather than storage details.
objectives: Read GetEmployeeClockEntries's real return type, IEnumerable<ClockEntry>, and explain exactly what capability that promises callers: enumeration, nothing else.
Explain why GetEmployeeClockEntries does NOT return List<ClockEntry>, even though its implementation is built from one.
Place List<T> in the interface hierarchy it implements: IList<T>, which implements ICollection<T>, which implements IEnumerable<T>.
Predict what capabilities are lost by declaring a return type as IEnumerable<T> instead of the concrete List<T> the method happens to build internally.

visuals.title: The real signature promises only enumeration
visuals.explanation: IEnumerable<ClockEntry> GetEmployeeClockEntries(...) -- callers can foreach over the result; nothing in the signature promises Count, indexing, or the ability to Add.

visuals.title: List<T> implements more than it exposes here
visuals.explanation: _clockEntries.Where(...) returns something that is enumerable, built from a List<ClockEntry> internally -- but the method's declared return type hides the List-specific members from callers.

visuals.title: The interface hierarchy is a chain of promises
visuals.explanation: IList<T> extends ICollection<T> extends IEnumerable<T> -- each step up adds capability (indexing, then adding/removing, on top of plain enumeration).

visuals.title: Narrower return types communicate intent
visuals.explanation: Returning IEnumerable<ClockEntry> tells callers 'treat this as read-only, enumerate it once' even though the concrete object underneath could support more.

preQuiz.prompt: Can a caller of GetEmployeeClockEntries call .Count on its return value directly, using only the declared IEnumerable<ClockEntry> type?
options: Not with a Count property -- IEnumerable<T> only guarantees enumeration; callers would need .Count() (the LINQ extension method, which itself enumerates) or to call .ToList() first for an indexable, countable collection
No -- IEnumerable<T> cannot be enumerated at all
preQuiz.explanation: IEnumerable<T>'s only member is GetEnumerator() -- Count, indexing, and Add all belong to interfaces further up the hierarchy (ICollection<T>, IList<T>) that GetEmployeeClockEntries's declared return type does not promise.

preQuiz.prompt: Why doesn't GetEmployeeClockEntries return List<ClockEntry>, even though .Where() is called on a List<ClockEntry> internally?
options: Returning the narrower IEnumerable<ClockEntry> tells callers exactly what they may rely on (enumeration) without promising list-specific capabilities (indexing, Add, Remove) that might not remain true if the implementation changes later
IEnumerable<T> is required by C# for any LINQ query result
List<ClockEntry> cannot be returned from a method
preQuiz.explanation: This is a deliberate narrowing: the real implementation happens to use a List internally, but the interface promises only what callers actually need -- read-only enumeration.

preQuiz.prompt: Where does IList<T> sit relative to IEnumerable<T> in the standard collection interface hierarchy?
options: IList<T> extends ICollection<T>, which extends IEnumerable<T> -- each interface adds capability on top of the one below it
IList<T> and IEnumerable<T> are unrelated interfaces
preQuiz.explanation: The hierarchy builds upward: plain enumeration (IEnumerable<T>), then add/remove/count (ICollection<T>), then indexing and insertion (IList<T>) -- List<T> implements all three.

concept.title: IEnumerable<ClockEntry> is a promise of enumeration, nothing more
paragraphs: The real GetEmployeeClockEntries signature is IEnumerable<ClockEntry> GetEmployeeClockEntries(int employeeId, DateTime startDate, DateTime endDate) -- confirmed directly against Interfaces/IClockEntryRepository.cs.

A caller holding this return value can foreach over it, or chain further LINQ methods (.Sum(), .OrderBy(), etc., all defined as extension methods on IEnumerable<T>) -- but cannot index into it with [0] or ask for .Count as a property, because IEnumerable<T> itself declares neither.
concept.code:
// Interfaces/IClockEntryRepository.cs -- the real signature
IEnumerable<ClockEntry> GetEmployeeClockEntries(int employeeId, DateTime startDate, DateTime endDate);

concept.title: The implementation returns more than the interface promises
paragraphs: ClockEntryRepository's real implementation is _clockEntries.Where(...) -- Where's actual runtime return type implements IEnumerable<ClockEntry> but is not a List<ClockEntry> at all; it is a compiler-generated iterator.

This is exactly why the interface, not the concrete implementation detail, is what callers should be written against: PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours never needed to know or care what concrete type Where actually returns.

concept.title: The hierarchy: IEnumerable<T>, ICollection<T>, IList<T>
paragraphs: List<ClockEntry> (ClockEntryRepository's actual backing storage) implements IList<ClockEntry>, which implements ICollection<ClockEntry>, which implements IEnumerable<ClockEntry>.

Each step adds capability: IEnumerable<T> for foreach; ICollection<T> adds Count, Add, Remove, Contains; IList<T> adds indexing ([int]) and Insert/RemoveAt. GetEmployeeClockEntries deliberately exposes only the bottom rung.
concept.code:
List<ClockEntry> _clockEntries;      // implements IList<ClockEntry>
IList<ClockEntry> asList = _clockEntries;          // indexing, Insert, RemoveAt
ICollection<ClockEntry> asCollection = _clockEntries; // Count, Add, Remove, Contains
IEnumerable<ClockEntry> asEnumerable = _clockEntries; // foreach only -- what GetEmployeeClockEntries actually returns

postQuiz.prompt: If PayrollService.CalculateTotalHours needed the count of an employee's clock entries as well as their sum, what would it need to do?
options: Call .ToList() on GetEmployeeClockEntries's result first (or use .Count(), the LINQ extension method, which re-enumerates), since IEnumerable<ClockEntry> alone has no Count property
Access ._clockEntries directly, since that already has Count
Nothing extra -- IEnumerable<T> already exposes Count
postQuiz.explanation: IEnumerable<T> genuinely has no Count property -- LINQ's .Count() extension method is a substitute that works by enumerating, not a shortcut to a property that was already there.

postQuiz.prompt: Why might ClockEntryRepository's internal choice of List<ClockEntry> change in the future (e.g. to a database-backed collection) without breaking PayrollService?
options: PayrollService only depends on IEnumerable<ClockEntry> (via IClockEntryRepository's interface), never on List<ClockEntry> specifically -- any implementation that can produce an IEnumerable<ClockEntry> satisfies the contract
PayrollService directly references List<ClockEntry> in its own code
It cannot change without breaking PayrollService
postQuiz.explanation: This is the same principle Session 20 taught about depending on interfaces -- here it applies one level deeper, to the collection type returned by an interface member.

postQuiz.prompt: What is the real reason GetEmployeeClockEntries's declared return type matters, if the actual object at runtime could support more?
options: It documents and enforces, at compile time, exactly what callers are allowed to assume -- protecting the implementation's freedom to change without callers noticing
Declared return types have no effect on what callers can do -- only the actual runtime type matters
It is purely a style preference with no functional consequence
postQuiz.explanation: C#'s static typing means the compiler enforces the DECLARED type's members, not the runtime type's full capability -- this is precisely the mechanism that makes narrow interfaces protect implementation freedom.

reflections: Why does GetEmployeeClockEntries's author choosing IEnumerable<ClockEntry> over List<ClockEntry> matter for anyone besides the method's own implementation?
What would you lose, as a caller, if every method in this codebase returned the most general possible type (object) instead of a specific interface?
Where else in this codebase does a method's declared return type deliberately hide more specific capability the implementation happens to have?
whatBreaks: Changing GetEmployeeClockEntries's declared return type to List<ClockEntry> would let callers start depending on list-specific members (indexing, Add) that the repository's author never intended to promise -- making a future change to the underlying storage a breaking change for those callers. Assuming IEnumerable<ClockEntry> supports indexing without first materializing it with .ToList() produces a compile error, not a runtime surprise -- exactly the kind of mistake the type system is built to catch early.
summary: GetEmployeeClockEntries's real, verified return type is IEnumerable<ClockEntry> -- a promise of enumeration only, even though its actual implementation is built from a List<ClockEntry>. The standard IEnumerable<T> -> ICollection<T> -> IList<T> hierarchy explains exactly what capability each step adds, and why a method's declared interface type, not its concrete backing type, is what callers should be written against.
